cloze.text: The gingiva provides a {{c1::tissue seal}} around the tooth and protects the underlying structures.
Gingival epithelium is a type of specialized {{c1::stratified squamous}} epithelium.
Biologic width includes the {{c1::junctional epithelium}} and the {{c2::connective tissue attachment}} to the tooth surface.
Free gingiva (marginal gingiva) is the {{c1::unattached}} portion of the gingiva near the gingival margin.
The free gingival groove is a slight depression that separates the {{c1::free (unattached)}} gingiva from the {{c2::attached}} gingiva.
cloze.extra: It may not be visible in some patients.

cloze.text: The free gingival groove corresponds to the depth of the {{c1::sulcus}}.
cloze.extra: It is not measured on the palate.

cloze.text: Attached gingiva lies between the {{c1::free gingival groove}} and the {{c2::mucogingival junction}}.
Attached gingiva is connected to the {{c1::cementum}} of the root and to the {{c2::periosteum}} of the alveolar bone.
cloze.extra: Periosteum = the connective tissue cover of the bone.

cloze.text: Oral pigmentation usually occurs on the {{c1::attached}} gingiva.
Attached gingiva is {{c1::keratinized}}, which gives better protection from daily activities such as chewing.
Attached gingiva is generally widest on the facial of the {{c1::maxillary anteriors}} and narrowest on the facial of the {{c2::mandibular premolars}}.
The mucogingival junction (MGJ) is the {{c1::apical}} boundary where the attached gingiva meets the {{c2::alveolar mucosa}}.
Alveolar mucosa is {{c1::red, smooth and shiny}} and {{c2::non-keratinized}}, whereas attached gingiva is coral pink and keratinized.
Interdental gingiva fills the area between two teeth and prevents {{c1::food and other irritants}} from becoming trapped.
Interdental gingiva is made of two interdental papillae, one {{c1::facial}} and one {{c1::lingual}}, connected by the {{c2::col}}.
The col is the gingiva directly {{c1::apical to (underneath)}} the contact point of two adjacent teeth, directed {{c2::bucco-lingually}}.
The col is not present if the adjacent teeth are {{c1::not in contact}} or if the gingiva has {{c2::receded}}.
The col consists of {{c1::non-keratinized}} tissue.
Sulcular epithelium lines the free gingival sulcus — the surface that faces the {{c1::tooth/root}}.
Sulcular epithelium extends from the crest of the {{c1::gingival margin}} to the {{c2::junctional epithelium}}.
Sulcular epithelium is {{c1::non-keratinized}}.
The permeability of the non-keratinized sulcular epithelium lets {{c1::gingival crevicular fluid (GCF)}} flow into the sulcus.
Gingival crevicular fluid is always present but {{c1::increases}} in disease.
The junctional epithelium (JE) forms the {{c1::base of the sulcus}} and provides a seal between the gingiva and the tooth surface.
Supragingival fibers of the gingiva are composed mainly of {{c1::collagen}} and {{c2::elastic}} fibers.
Supragingival fibers: {{c1::Alveologingival}} fibers run from the alveolar crest to the gingiva; function: {{c2::attach gingiva to bone}}.

cloze.text: Supragingival fibers: {{c1::Circular}} fibers encircle the tooth like a ring; function: {{c2::support the free gingiva}}.

cloze.extra: Language Builder: the first part of the name = origin, the second = destination (dento- = tooth, -gingival = gingiva); inter- = between, trans- = across/through.

cloze.text: Supragingival fibers: {{c1::Transseptal}} fibers run from the cementum of one tooth over the alveolar crest to the cementum of the adjacent tooth; function: {{c2::connect adjacent teeth to one another}}.
cloze.extra: Language Builder: the first part of the name = origin, the second = destination (dento- = tooth, -gingival = gingiva); inter- = between, trans- = across/through.

cloze.text: The PDL connects the tooth ({{c1::cementum}}) to the {{c2::alveolar bone}} of the tooth socket.
The {{c1::supportive}} function of the PDL suspends the tooth in its socket and absorbs the impact of forces.
The {{c1::sensory}} function of the PDL detects pressure and pain.
The {{c1::nutritive}} function of the PDL carries nutrients from blood vessels to the cementum, bone and gingiva.
The {{c1::formative}} function of the PDL builds and maintains cementum and bone; the PDL contains {{c2::cementoblasts}} and {{c2::osteoblasts}}.
The {{c1::resorptive}} function of the PDL remodels the alveolar bone in response to pressure (e.g., braces).
The PDL has a rich supply of {{c1::nerves}} and {{c1::blood vessels}}.
{{c1::Fibroblasts}} are the most prominent cells of the PDL.
Teeth that are accidentally exfoliated can be re-implanted into the socket if damage to the {{c1::periodontal ligament}} is minimal.
PDL fibers: the {{c1::alveolar crest}} group runs diagonally downward from the cementum to the alveolar crest and resists {{c2::horizontal movement}} of the tooth.
PDL fibers: the {{c1::horizontal}} group runs horizontally from the cementum to the bone just apical to the alveolar crest fibers and resists {{c2::horizontal pressure}}.
PDL fibers: the {{c1::oblique}} group runs diagonally downward from the bone to the cementum and resists {{c2::vertical pressure}}.
cloze.extra: Oblique = the largest and most significant PDL fiber group.

cloze.text: The largest and most significant PDL fiber group is the {{c1::oblique}} group.
PDL fibers: the {{c1::apical}} group extends from the apex of the tooth to the bone and resists forces that {{c2::pull the tooth out of the socket}}.
PDL fibers: the {{c1::interradicular}} group extends from the cementum in the furcation to the interradicular septum and stabilizes the tooth; it is present only in {{c2::multirooted}} teeth.
Cementum is a thin layer of mineralized tissue made of {{c1::hydroxyapatite}} crystals that covers the {{c2::root}} of a tooth.
cloze.extra: Hydroxyapatite = calcium and phosphate.

cloze.text: Cementum is {{c1::light yellow}} in color.
Cementum is where the {{c1::PDL}} connects the tooth to the alveolar bone (via Sharpey's fibers).
{{c1::Trauma}} and {{c1::infection}} may thicken the cementum.
cloze.extra: Thickened cementum = hypercementosis (see figure).

cloze.text: Cementum receives its nutrients from the {{c1::PDL}}; it contains no {{c2::blood vessels or nerves}}.
At the CEJ, the cementum most often {{c1::overlaps}} the enamel; less often it {{c2::meets}} the enamel; rarely there is a {{c3::gap}} between them.
The continuous cycle of bone breakdown (resorption) and rebuilding (formation) is called {{c1::bone remodeling}}.
cloze.extra: It is essential for maintaining bone health and adapting to stress.

cloze.text: The presence of alveolar bone depends on the {{c1::teeth}}: if teeth are lost, the bone {{c2::resorbs}}, leading to a loss of ridge dimensions.
Alveolar bone gives direct support to the teeth and is critical for maintaining {{c1::tooth position}} and {{c2::masticatory function}}.
The alveolus (tooth socket) is lined by the {{c1::cribriform plate}}.
Alveolar bone proper is a thin layer of {{c1::compact}} bone that lines the tooth socket.
Alveolar bone proper has numerous holes through which blood vessels and nerves connect the {{c1::PDL}} to the {{c2::cancellous bone}}.
Alveolar bone proper is called the {{c1::cribriform plate}} because of its sieve-like appearance and the {{c2::lamina dura}} radiographically.
On a radiograph the lamina dura appears as a distinct, thin {{c1::white}} line.
Alveolar bone proper forms the inner wall of the socket and provides attachment for the {{c1::PDL fibers}}.
Cortical bone is a layer of {{c1::compact, dense}} bone forming the outer wall of the alveolar process on the {{c2::facial and lingual}} sides.
cloze.extra: Provides strength and protection to the alveolar process.

cloze.text: Cortical bone does not show on radiographs in the {{c1::maxilla}} because it is thin; it is thicker and more visible in the {{c2::mandible}}.
Cancellous bone is the {{c1::spongy}}, lattice-like bone that fills the interior of the alveolar process, between the {{c2::cortical plates}} and the {{c3::alveolar bone proper}}.
cloze.extra: Also called trabecular bone. Many holes for blood vessels and nerves; porous, web-like appearance.

cloze.text: Cancellous (spongy) bone is also known as {{c1::trabecular}} bone.
Cancellous bone provides metabolic support and acts as a reservoir for {{c1::bone marrow}}.
The alveolar crest is the most {{c1::coronal}} portion of the alveolar process (its highest point).
The {{c1::alveolar crest}} is the first bone to be destroyed in periodontal disease, and a key radiographic indicator of periodontal health/disease.
The periosteum is a layer of {{c1::connective soft tissue}} that covers the outer surface of bone, except the {{c2::articular surfaces}}.
cloze.extra: It contains blood vessels and nerves that nourish the bone.

cloze.text: The periosteum is essential for bone {{c1::growth}}, {{c1::repair}} and {{c1::nourishment}}, and protects the bone.
Healthy gingiva is {{c1::coral pink}} in color; {{c2::melanin}} pigmentation may be present.
Healthy gingiva has a {{c1::firm and resilient}} consistency.
Healthy attached gingiva has a {{c1::stippled (orange-peel)}} appearance because of the firm binding of the fibers to the alveolar bone.
In health the gingival margin has a {{c1::scalloped}} outline.
Healthy interdental papillae are {{c1::knife-edged and pointed}} and fill the embrasure space.
Healthy gingiva shows {{c1::no bleeding}} upon probing.
In health the junctional epithelium is firmly attached to the tooth by {{c1::hemidesmosomes}}.
In health the alveolar crest is {{c1::1–2 mm}} apical to the base of the {{c2::junctional epithelium}}.
cloze.extra: Book p.89 also gives 1–2 mm apical to the CEJ.

cloze.text: {{c1::Dental plaque biofilm}} is the primary etiology of periodontal diseases.

Gingival inflammation and periodontal destruction can also occur or be worsened by {{c1::hormonal changes}}, {{c1::systemic diseases}} or {{c1::genetic disorders}} that modify the "{{c2::host factor}}".
Gingivitis is a {{c1::reversible}} inflammatory condition of the gingiva.
Gingivitis is typically observed clinically within {{c1::4–14 days}} after plaque accumulation in the gingival sulcus.
Gingivitis can present as {{c1::localized}} or {{c1::generalized}}.
{{c1::Acute}} gingivitis has a sudden onset and short duration; {{c2::chronic}} gingivitis persists for months or years.
Gingivitis: the gingiva is red/erythematous due to {{c1::increased blood flow}}; if persistent, congestion can give a {{c2::bluish/purple}} hue.
Gingivitis consistency: {{c1::edematous (swollen/spongy)}} in acute forms; may become {{c2::fibrotic (leathery, firm)}} in chronic forms due to collagen formation.
{{c1::Bleeding upon gentle probing}} is a hallmark sign of gingivitis.
In gingivitis the gingival margin is usually {{c1::rolled or blunted}}, losing its normal knife-edged adaptation.
In gingivitis the interdental papillae are {{c1::bulbous and swollen}}, often filling the embrasure space.
In gingivitis probing depths are typically {{c1::4 mm or greater}} because of swelling of the gingival margin, {{c2::without}} apical migration of the junctional epithelium.
In gingivitis the junctional epithelium stays at or {{c1::coronal}} to the CEJ — there is no apical migration.
Gingivitis shows {{c1::no radiographic changes}} — there is no bone loss.
Periodontitis is an {{c1::irreversible}} inflammatory disease characterized by {{c2::loss of clinical attachment}} due to destruction of the periodontium.
Unlike gingivitis, periodontitis damages the supporting {{c1::alveolar bone}} and {{c1::periodontal ligament}}.
Periodontitis can be localized or generalized, based on the extent of {{c1::attachment loss}}.
The severity, complexity and rate of progression of periodontitis are determined by the {{c1::AAP Staging and Grading}} system.

Under current AAP classification, common forms include {{c1::biofilm-induced periodontitis}}, {{c2::necrotizing periodontal diseases}}, and {{c3::periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic diseases}}.
The clinical appearance of the gingiva {{c1::is NOT a reliable indicator}} of the presence, severity or extent of periodontitis.
Periodontitis: tissues can look dark bluish-purplish or red; in chronic cases they may look {{c1::light pink}} because new {{c2::collagen fiber}} production masks the inflammation.
Periodontitis: consistency can be {{c1::edematous}} (spongy, swollen, smooth, shiny) or {{c2::fibrotic}} (leathery, firm) in chronic conditions.
In periodontitis the gingival margin is typically {{c1::swollen or fibrotic}}, losing its knife-edged adaptation.
In periodontitis interdental papillae are often blunted and may no longer fill the embrasure because of {{c1::destruction}} and {{c1::recession}}.
Periodontitis: bleeding upon gentle probing is common, and/or {{c1::suppuration (pus)}} may be present.
In periodontitis probing depths are {{c1::4 mm or greater}} due to inflammation and, critically, {{c2::apical migration of the junctional epithelium}}.
The presence of a periodontal pocket indicates a {{c1::history}} of infection, not necessarily current activity.
The defining characteristic of periodontitis is {{c1::apical migration of the junctional epithelium}} along the root surface.
Pain in periodontitis is often {{c1::absent}} — the disease can progress silently.
cloze.extra: "Mother Nature blew it!"

cloze.text: In periodontitis the alveolar bone is {{c1::permanently destroyed}}; radiographically evident bone loss is a key diagnostic feature.
{{c1::Tooth mobility}} may be present in periodontitis because of bone loss.
{{c1::Horizontal}} bone loss is the most common pattern and results in a {{c2::suprabony}} pocket.
{{c1::Vertical (angular)}} bone loss is less common and results in an {{c2::infrabony}} pocket.
In a suprabony pocket the base of the pocket is {{c1::coronal to (above)}} the alveolar bone crest.
cloze.extra: Supra- = above. Bone is reduced uniformly.

cloze.text: In an infrabony pocket the base of the pocket is {{c1::apical to (below)}} the alveolar crest, forming within a trench-like bone defect.
cloze.extra: Infra- = below. Bone loss is uneven.

basic.front: Why can bone be resorbed (e.g., during tooth movement) without the root being resorbed?

basic.front: Which cementum-enamel relationship can cause dentinal hypersensitivity?

mcq.question: While probing, the hygienist pulls the patient's lip and watches where the tissue begins to move. Which landmark is she locating?
mcq.explanation: The MGJ separates the firmly attached gingiva from the movable alveolar mucosa; moving the lip shows where movable mucosa begins. The free gingival groove separates free from attached gingiva and does not move with the lip.

mcq.question: Which supragingival fiber group runs from the cementum of one tooth, over the alveolar crest, to the cementum of the adjacent tooth?
mcq.explanation: Trans- = across: transseptal fibers cross over the interdental septum (alveolar crest) from tooth to tooth. Intercircular fibers also link teeth but encircle several teeth rather than crossing the crest.

mcq.question: A patient in orthodontic treatment asks how braces move her teeth through bone. Which PDL function is mainly responsible?
mcq.explanation: The resorptive function remodels alveolar bone in response to pressure (e.g., braces). The supportive function only suspends the tooth and absorbs forces.

mcq.question: Which PDL fiber group bears most of the vertical force of chewing?
mcq.explanation: Oblique fibers are the largest and most significant group and resist vertical pressure. Horizontal fibers resist horizontal (sideways) pressure.

mcq.question: On a periapical radiograph, the thin white line outlining the tooth socket is the radiographic image of which structure?
mcq.explanation: Alveolar bone proper (cribriform plate) appears radiographically as the lamina dura. Cortical bone is the outer facial/lingual wall and is often not seen in the maxilla.

mcq.question: Which bone is the first to be destroyed in periodontal disease?
options: B. Cortical bone of the mandible
D. Cancellous bone around the apex
mcq.explanation: The alveolar crest, the most coronal part of the alveolar process, is the first bone lost and a key radiographic indicator. Apical cancellous bone is affected only later.

mcq.question: A patient has red, bulbous papillae that bleed on gentle probing and 4-mm probing depths. Radiographs show no bone loss and the junctional epithelium is at the CEJ. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Probing depth is increased only by gingival swelling, with no apical migration of the JE and no bone loss — gingivitis. Periodontitis requires loss of attachment (apical migration of the JE).

mcq.question: Which finding defines periodontitis rather than gingivitis?
options: C. Apical migration of the junctional epithelium
mcq.answer: C. Apical migration of the junctional epithelium
mcq.explanation: Apical migration of the JE (loss of attachment) is the defining characteristic of periodontitis. A 4-mm probing depth also occurs in gingivitis from swelling alone, without JE migration.

mcq.question: A radiograph shows uneven, trench-like bone loss along the mesial root of #19, and the probe tip passes apical to the alveolar crest. This pocket is best described as:
options: A. Suprabony pocket from horizontal bone loss
B. Infrabony pocket from vertical (angular) bone loss
D. Gingival pocket without attachment loss
mcq.answer: B. Infrabony pocket from vertical (angular) bone loss
mcq.explanation: A pocket whose base lies apical to the crest, inside an uneven angular defect, is infrabony. A suprabony pocket has its base coronal to the crest, with uniform horizontal loss.
